screens.title: Advanced Scripting Patterns & Design
screens.subtitle: Singleton, Observer, and State Machine for robust Unity code

narration.text: In this lesson we’ll build professional Unity code structure by learning three essential patterns: Singleton for globally accessible managers, Observer for event-driven decoupling, and State Machines for clear behavior logic. These patterns are practical tools, not academic exercises. You will see why teams use them to make projects easier to maintain, easier to test, and faster to extend. For example, a GameManager implemented as a Singleton gives you one reliable place to start or stop the game, while an Observer lets UI elements react automatically when player health changes. A State Machine keeps AI or animation logic predictable by separating each behavior into its own defined state. We’ll also cover trade-offs and common mistakes, like creating Singletons that duplicate across scenes or forgetting to unsubscribe from events. You’ll practice by wiring an AudioManager and a SettingsManager so volume changes flow from a settings slider to any playing sound. By the end you should understand when each pattern is appropriate, how to implement it in C# and Unity, and how to avoid the pitfalls that turn useful patterns into fragile code. Think about a system in your project that feels messy now — this lesson gives methods to make it clean and testable.

keyIdea.title: Patterns enable maintainable Unity code
keyIdea.text: Use Singletons for global managers, Observer for event-driven decoupling, and State Machines for predictable behavior; each has trade-offs to manage.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide hands-on practice and assessment. First, you will understand why design patterns matter in game development: they are repeatable solutions that reduce coupling and improve maintainability. I will show concrete examples so you can see the patterns in action. Second, you will implement the Singleton pattern for managers that need a single, globally accessible instance. Practically this means writing an Awake check, setting a static Instance property, and using DontDestroyOnLoad when persistence between scenes is required. Third, you will apply the Observer pattern to decouple systems. You will create events, have listeners subscribe and unsubscribe correctly, and see how UI and game logic react without direct references. Finally, you will design and implement a basic State Machine for character or AI behavior, organizing behaviors into named states and using clear transitions. Each objective is paired with a competency milestone so you can verify your implementation. These skills matter because games quickly become hard to change without structure; these patterns give you predictable, testable building blocks.

screens.title: What is a design pattern?
screens.subtitle: A practical definition and why it matters in games

narration.text: A design pattern is a reusable solution to a recurring software design problem. In games, patterns capture engineering intent: how managers should be accessed, how systems should notify each other, or how behaviors should switch. This matters because games are complex systems that evolve. Without patterns, code tends to become tightly coupled—scripts know too much about each other and changing one system breaks another. Design patterns provide a blueprint that teams can read and follow, reducing guesswork when onboarding new members or debugging runtime issues. Concretely, think of a pattern as a small recipe. The Singleton recipe says: keep one instance and provide a global point of access. The Observer recipe says: publish state changes and let many subscribers react. The State Machine recipe says: name each behavior and define transition rules. A common misconception is that patterns are one-size-fits-all. They are not; they introduce structure and sometimes boilerplate, so choose based on trade-offs. For example, Singletons simplify access but can hide dependencies; Observers decouple but require careful unsubscribe logic. Before applying a pattern, ask whether it reduces complexity or just shifts it. Can you write a simple test for the change? If yes, the pattern is likely helping.

keyIdea.title: Design patterns are practical recipes
keyIdea.text: Use patterns to express intent, reduce coupling, and improve maintainability—apply them where they simplify tests and team work.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › What is a design pattern?
Definition
A reusable solution to a common problem in software design that captures intent and structure.
• Patterns make code predictable and easier to read across a team.
• They help you identify where responsibilities belong and how systems communicate.
• Misuse can hide dependencies or add unnecessary boilerplate.
Analogy
Patterns are like recipes: follow steps for a reliable result, but substitute only when you understand the trade-offs.
Key Takeaway

Apply patterns when they reduce cognitive load and make testing or collaboration simpler; avoid them when they mask dependencies.

Common patterns in this chapter
Singleton
One instance manager.
Observer
Publish-subscribe events.
State Machine
Named states and transitions.
Check your understanding
Name a component in your project that would benefit from a pattern and explain which one and why.

screens.title: The Singleton pattern
screens.subtitle: What it guarantees and common uses in Unity

narration.text: The Singleton pattern guarantees that a class has only one instance and provides a global access point to it. In Unity this frequently becomes a MonoBehaviour that sets a static Instance reference in Awake, checks for duplicates, and optionally calls DontDestroyOnLoad to persist across scenes. Common use cases include managers such as GameManager, AudioManager, InputManager, or SaveLoadManager—systems that coordinate global state or services. The strength of a Singleton is its simplicity: any script can obtain the manager via the Instance property rather than wiring references through scenes. That convenience can also be a weakness. Overusing Singletons can lead to hidden dependencies where many scripts implicitly rely on a global object, which makes unit testing harder and increases coupling. A common mistake is not handling scene loads: when you reload a scene with a manager prefab, duplicates can be created unless Awake checks remove extra instances. Another pitfall is storing transient data in a persistent Singleton, which can lead to unexpected state across scenes. Use Singletons for orchestrating global services, keep their public surface small, and prefer explicit dependency injection for large, test-sensitive systems. How would you make your critical manager safe across scene loads?

keyIdea.title: Singleton: single instance, global access
keyIdea.text: Use for managers that should persist and be accessible globally, but avoid hidden global dependencies and duplicate instances.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › The Singleton pattern
Singleton guarantees
One instance, global retrieval, optional persistence across scene loads.
• Use for coordinating cross-scene services like audio or saving.
• Keep the API narrow to reduce coupling. Avoid storing lots of mutable global state.
• Testability: Singletons are harder to mock; add abstraction when unit testing matters.
Common mistake
Forgetting to remove duplicate instances on scene load can create conflicting state and runtime errors.
Key Takeaway

Use Singletons for small, well-defined global services and protect them against duplicates and hidden state across scenes.

When to prefer a Singleton
• Systems that must be reachable from many places and have a single authoritative source.
• Small service APIs where mocking is not a primary concern.
Concrete example
An AudioManager holds an AudioSource and exposes PlaySound. Any object can call the manager to play a clip without wiring references through scene hierarchies.
Misconception
Singletons are not a substitute for proper architecture. They solve access, not design. Overuse can hide coupling.

narration.text: Let's walk through a safe Singleton implementation that you can reuse in Unity projects. The key steps are: declare a public static Instance property, set it in Awake, check for an existing instance and destroy duplicates, and call DontDestroyOnLoad when you want the manager to persist across scenes. In practice you put checks in Awake so the Unity lifecycle resolves duplicates early. When destroying duplicates, log a warning so you can spot unwanted prefab duplication during development. Also, initialize any required components after establishing the instance so other scripts accessing the Instance get a ready object. For example, a GameManager sets Instance in Awake, calls DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject), and exposes public control methods like StartGame. A common oversight is performing heavy initialization before instance checks, which can leave temporary objects running. Another issue is failing to null out static references on domain reload in the editor; consider clearing Instance in OnDestroy. As a test, load and unload scenes while watching the console: you should see a single initialization message and no duplicate warnings in a correct implementation. How would you adjust this pattern if you needed multiple instances for different game modes?

keyIdea.title: Safe Awake checks and persistence
keyIdea.text: Set Instance early, destroy duplicates, persist intentionally, and initialize components after the single instance is confirmed.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Implementing a safe Singleton
Code walkthrough
Follow this pattern to avoid duplicates and persist managers safely.
// GameManager: safe Singleton pattern
public class GameManager : MonoBehaviour
{
    public static GameManager Instance { get; private set; }

    private void Awake()
    {
        if (Instance != null && Instance != this)
        {
            Debug.LogWarning("Duplicate GameManager detected. Destroying new instance.");
            Destroy(gameObject);
            return;
        }

        Instance = this;
        DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject);
        Debug.Log("GameManager initialized.");
    }

    public void StartGame() { /* start logic */ }
}
Example check
Load a scene that contains the manager prefab twice and confirm the console shows a single initialization message and a duplicate warning when the second prefab is discovered and destroyed.
Best practices
  • Keep public surface minimal to avoid implicit coupling.
  • Call DontDestroyOnLoad only when persistence is required.
  • Log instance creation and duplicates for easier debugging.
  • Clear static Instance on domain reload or OnDestroy when appropriate.
Misconception
A Singleton does not automatically make a good architecture. Use it wisely and keep responsibilities focused.

narration.text: The Observer pattern creates a one-to-many relationship where a publisher broadcasts state changes and any number of subscribers react. In Unity, this commonly appears as static C# events or delegate fields that other MonoBehaviours subscribe to in OnEnable and unsubscribe in OnDisable. The primary value is decoupling: publishers do not need to know who listens. A practical example is PlayerHealth publishing a HealthChanged event. The health bar UI, a damage indicator, and a game over manager can all subscribe independently and react when the player's health changes. A critical implementation detail is correct subscription lifecycle management. Forgetting to unsubscribe when an object is destroyed leaves a stale reference on the event, which can cause memory leaks, null reference exceptions, or unexpected behavior when the event fires. Always unsubscribe in OnDisable or OnDestroy. Another misconception is to overuse global events for everything; use them for cross-cutting concerns, not for local interactions inside the same component. Finally, name events clearly and include relevant data in the event payload so subscribers have the information they need without reaching back into the publisher. How will you ensure subscribers clean up after themselves in your scenes?

keyIdea.title: Observer: decoupled notifications
keyIdea.text: Publish state changes and have multiple subscribers react independently; always manage subscription lifecycles to avoid leaks.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › The Observer pattern
Publish-Subscribe
Publish events when state changes and let subscribers react independently.
• Use static events or delegate fields for cross-component updates.
• Subscribe in OnEnable and unsubscribe in OnDisable to avoid leaks.
• Pass concise, relevant data in the event so subscribers don’t query the publisher.
Concrete example
PlayerHealth publishes OnHealthChanged with an int value. HealthUI subscribes and updates visuals when the event fires.
Common pitfalls
  • Not unsubscribing leads to callbacks on destroyed objects.
  • Overusing global events increases implicit coupling across your project.
  • Using events without clear payloads forces subscribers to reach back into publishers for data.
Key Takeaway
Observers decouple systems but require disciplined subscription management and clear event design.

screens.title: Observer implementation: PlayerHealth and HealthUI
screens.subtitle: C# events: subscribe, publish, and unsubscribe safely

narration.text: We will step through a simple Observer implementation using a PlayerHealth publisher and a HealthUI subscriber. The publisher defines a static event that sends the current health value. When the health changes, the publisher invokes the event, and any subscribers receive the new value. On the subscriber side, subscribe in OnEnable and unsubscribe in OnDisable so you never leave dangling subscriptions. This lifecycle behavior prevents events from calling into destroyed objects and prevents surprises during scene unloading. A concrete example: PlayerHealth holds a CurrentHealth property. When TakeDamage reduces health, it invokes the event with the new value. HealthUI registers a callback that updates the displayed value. A common mistake is subscribing in Start and unsubscribing in OnDestroy only; if a subscriber is disabled and re-enabled, it may register multiple times. If you see duplicate updates, check your subscription points. Also avoid storing heavy references in the event payload; send minimal necessary data. After implementing this pattern, test by applying damage and watching console logs or UI updates. Do you see the expected single update per event, and does disabling a UI object stop its updates?

keyIdea.title: Subscribe and unsubscribe correctly
keyIdea.text: Publish minimal state and manage subscriber lifecycle using OnEnable and OnDisable to avoid leaks and duplicate callbacks.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Observer implementation
Publisher: PlayerHealth
using System;

public class PlayerHealth : MonoBehaviour
{
    public static event Action OnHealthChanged;
    private int _currentHealth = 100;

    public int CurrentHealth
    {
        get => _currentHealth;
        private set
        {
            if (_currentHealth == value) return;
            _currentHealth = value;
            OnHealthChanged?.Invoke(_currentHealth);
            Debug.Log($"Player health changed to: {_currentHealth}");
        }
    }

    public void TakeDamage(int amount) { CurrentHealth = Mathf.Max(0, CurrentHealth - amount); }
}
Subscriber: HealthUI
public class HealthUI : MonoBehaviour
{
    void OnEnable()  { PlayerHealth.OnHealthChanged += UpdateHealthDisplay; }
    void OnDisable() { PlayerHealth.OnHealthChanged -= UpdateHealthDisplay; }

    void UpdateHealthDisplay(int health) { Debug.Log($"UI: Displaying health: {health}"); }
}
Common mistake
Subscribing multiple times (for example in Start without unsubscribing on disable) causes duplicate callbacks. Use OnEnable/OnDisable for consistent lifecycle behavior.

screens.title: Observer pitfalls and alternatives
screens.subtitle: When to use events and when to prefer direct references

narration.text: Observer events are powerful but not always the best solution. Use events when multiple independent systems need to react to a single change, such as a health change that drives UI updates, sound effects, and game over logic. However, if the interaction is local or tightly coupled—say a weapon directly updating its owner’s ammo display—a direct reference or method call may be simpler and less error-prone. Another consideration is debugging: events scatter behavior across subscribers, which can make tracing the source of an action harder. Use clear naming and consistent payloads to reduce this friction. Memory management is the main practical pitfall. A subscriber that fails to unsubscribe may keep a delegate alive, preventing garbage collection. This is especially relevant in scenes with frequent object creation or destruction. If you need stronger guarantees, consider using weak event patterns or a centralized event broker that manages lifetimes. Finally, avoid broadcasting large objects on events; prefer compact data like an integer or a small struct. This reduces coupling and makes listeners easier to reason about. As you design events, ask whether subscribers truly need global broadcast or if a local reference is clearer and safer.

keyIdea.title: Use events judiciously
keyIdea.text: Prefer Observer for many-to-many decoupling; prefer direct references for local, tightly coupled interactions and always manage subscriptions.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Observer pitfalls
When events shine
  • Multiple systems react to the same state change.
  • Loose coupling improves reuse and independent modification.
  • Event-driven UI updates without tight scene wiring.
Alternatives
Direct method calls or references for local interactions, or a broker for complex lifetimes.
Pitfalls & fixes
• Forgetting to unsubscribe keeps dead references alive. Unsubscribe in OnDisable. • Overuse spreads logic and makes debugging harder. Use events for cross-cutting concerns only. • Sending large objects couples publishers and subscribers. Send minimal payloads.
Quick fix

If you see repeated callbacks, check subscription points, prefer OnEnable/OnDisable, and add clear logging to trace the publisher.

narration.text: A State Machine organizes behavior by giving an object a finite set of named states and rules for transitioning between them. In Unity this is often implemented with an enum for the states and a switch or dedicated state classes to handle per-state logic. This approach eliminates sprawling Update methods filled with nested conditionals and makes behavior easy to reason about. For AI or character control, common states include Idle, Patrol, Attack, Flee, and Dead. Each state defines what the object does when active, and transition rules determine when to change states. This makes debugging simpler: you can log state entries and exits and watch transitions in the console or inspector. A simple pitfall is over-complicating transitions. Start with clear, minimal rules and only introduce more complex state scaffolding when needed. Another misconception is that enums are always sufficient; for complex behaviors with many transitions and entry/exit actions, separate state classes provide better encapsulation. As a test, implement an enemy that patrols until a player is near, then switches to Attack, and returns to Patrol when the player leaves. Notice how the switch statement centralizes the transition logic and how each state's code becomes smaller and easier to test. What state would you add next to make behavior feel more lifelike?

keyIdea.title: State Machine: clear states and transitions
keyIdea.text: Use enums or state classes to separate behavior and make transitions explicit, reducing complex conditionals and easing debugging.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › State Machine pattern
What a State Machine gives you
Readable behavior, explicit transitions, and smaller per-state code blocks.
• Define a finite set of states representing distinct behaviors.
• Implement per-state logic and clear rules for transitions.
• Improve debugging by logging state changes and entry/exit actions.
Concrete example
EnemyAI with states Idle, Patrol, Attack, Flee. Transitions depend on player proximity and internal conditions like health.
Pitfalls
• Too many ad-hoc transitions make the state graph hard to follow. Keep a simple map of allowed transitions. • Putting all logic in Update instead of isolated state methods recreates the original complexity. Encapsulate per-state behavior.
Key Takeaway

Make states explicit and transitions predictable. Start simple and refactor to state classes as complexity grows.

screens.title: State Machine in code: EnemyAI example
screens.subtitle: Enum states and a switch-based update loop

narration.text: This walkthrough shows a compact State Machine using an enum and a switch statement to control behavior. The pattern keeps the Update loop simple: evaluate the current state and call its handler. Each handler implements the behavior for that state and can set the current state to trigger transitions. For example, an EnemyAI enum includes Idle, Patrol, Attack, and Flee. Patrol moves the enemy along waypoints while Attack chases and applies damage. When the player is too far away, Attack switches back to Patrol. Implementing transitions in the state handlers makes the logic explicit and localized. A concrete implementation logs state changes so you can confirm transitions when testing. Use small helper methods to keep handlers readable and avoid long Update blocks. If your state logic grows, extract each state to its own class to improve testability. Also consider how external events, like being stunned or receiving a target, should request state changes rather than tightly coupling the state handlers to external systems. After implementing this simple switch-based machine, test by moving the player and watching the console for state entry logs. Did each transition occur exactly when expected?

keyIdea.title: Enum + switch for clear transitions
keyIdea.text: Use a switch on an enum to separate state handlers; log transitions and refactor to state classes as complexity grows.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › State Machine in code
Enum-based State Machine
public class EnemyAI : MonoBehaviour
{
    public enum EnemyState { Idle, Patrol, Attack, Flee }
    public EnemyState currentState = EnemyState.Idle;

    void Update()
    {
        switch (currentState)
        {
            case EnemyState.Idle: HandleIdleState(); break;
            case EnemyState.Patrol: HandlePatrolState(); break;
            case EnemyState.Attack: HandleAttackState(); break;
            case EnemyState.Flee: HandleFleeState(); break;
        }
    }

    void HandleIdleState() { /* transitions to Patrol or Attack */ }
    void HandlePatrolState() { /* patrol movement */ }
    void HandleAttackState() { /* chase and attack */ }
    void HandleFleeState() { /* run away */ }
}
Testing and instrumentation
Log state entries and transitions. Trigger transitions in editor by moving a test player to ensure behavior is predictable and that states revert correctly. If transitions grow complex, refactor into state classes with entry and exit methods for clarity.
Misconception
A state machine is not only for AI; use it for complex UI flows or game state where explicit transitions improve clarity.

narration.text: This integration shows how Singleton and Observer work together in a small, testable system. The AudioManager is a Singleton that persists across scenes and owns an AudioSource. SettingsManager publishes an event when MasterVolume changes. AudioManager subscribes to that event and updates the AudioSource volume. The workflow is simple: the UI slider updates SettingsManager. MasterVolume, SettingsManager invokes OnMasterVolumeChanged with the new float value, and AudioManager’s handler sets its audio source volume accordingly. This decouples UI from audio logic — the slider does not need a direct reference to the audio source. Implementation notes: create an empty GameObject named _Managers and add both managers. Make AudioManager a Singleton with Awake checks and DontDestroyOnLoad. In AudioManager’s OnEnable subscribe to SettingsManager. OnMasterVolumeChanged and unsubscribe in OnDisable. Test by moving the slider and observing debug logs and audio volume changes in the inspector. A common mistake is subscribing before the Instance is ready; ensure the Singleton is initialized before other systems attempt to subscribe. After you wire this, you’ll have a small but robust example of patterns cooperating to give clean runtime behavior. Integrating patterns: AudioManager + SettingsManager means singletons provide access and persistence; observers decouple notifications. combined, they let ui drive services without tight wiring.. In practical terms, hands-on activity architecture and wiring. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Patterns together form clean architecture
keyIdea.text: Singletons provide access and persistence; Observers decouple notifications. Combined, they let UI drive services without tight wiring.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › AudioManager + SettingsManager
Architecture
Managers live under a single _Managers GameObject. AudioManager is a Singleton and subscribes to volume changes from SettingsManager.
AudioManager (Singleton)
Persists across scenes, exposes PlaySound, subscribes to OnMasterVolumeChanged.
SettingsManager (Observer)
Publishes MasterVolume changes via a static event.
Hands-on steps
  1. Create _Managers GameObject and attach both scripts.
  2. Make AudioManager a Singleton and ensure an AudioSource is present.
  3. In SettingsManager, define OnMasterVolumeChanged and invoke it when MasterVolume is set.
  4. Subscribe in AudioManager.OnEnable and unsubscribe in OnDisable to update volume.
Concrete example
Move the slider, check console logs for the volume event, and watch AudioSource.volume update. If no change appears, verify subscriptions and that the Singleton is initialized.
Key Takeaway

This small integration demonstrates how patterns compose: Singletons for access, Observers for notifications, resulting in flexible, testable behavior.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Compact definitions to keep in mind

narration.text: Summarize the essentials so they stick. A Design Pattern is a reusable solution to a common design problem and helps structure code for teams and long-lived projects. The Singleton Pattern guarantees a single instance and a global access point—use it for small, well-defined managers but guard against duplicates and hidden dependencies. The Observer Pattern provides publish-subscribe behavior so multiple systems can react to state changes without direct references; always unsubscribe to avoid leaks. These core concepts help you design systems that are maintainable, debuggable, and easier to test. Keep these short definitions in mind as you implement the lab and judge when a pattern helps rather than complicates the design. Key Concepts means design pattern, singleton, and observer are practical tools—use them intentionally and mind the trade-offs.. In practical terms, compact definitions to keep in mind. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Remember these quick definitions
keyIdea.text: Design Pattern, Singleton, and Observer are practical tools—use them intentionally and mind the trade-offs.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Key Concepts
Design Pattern
A reusable solution to a common problem that expresses intent and structure.
Singleton
One instance with global access. Use for small managers and protect against duplicates.
Observer
Publish-subscribe events let many listeners react without direct references.
Takeaway

Patterns make systems easier to reason about when used intentionally. Pair them with logging and tests to confirm behavior in runtime and across scene changes.

screens.title: Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact cards to recall during coding

narration.text: Keep this quick reference nearby while you code. First: Singletons give global access but can hide dependencies—use them for managers and protect against duplicates with Awake checks and DontDestroyOnLoad. Second: Observers decouple systems via events; always subscribe and unsubscribe cleanly to avoid leaks and duplicated callbacks. Third: State Machines make behavior explicit—start with enums and switch handlers and refactor to state classes when behavior becomes complex. These three reminders will help you choose the right tool at the right time and avoid the most common implementation mistakes. Quick Reference means singleton: one, accessible, persistent; observer: publish and unsubscribe; state machine: explicit states and transitions.. In practical terms, three compact cards to recall during coding. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Quick Reference
Singleton
One instance, Awake checks, DontDestroyOnLoad when needed.
Observer
Publish updates and unsubscribe in OnDisable to avoid leaks.
State Machine
Explicit states and transitions keep behavior predictable.
Final Tip

Use logging and simple tests to confirm your pattern implementations behave correctly across scene loads and object lifecycle events.

ai_generation_note: Create a 12-minute mixed media lesson. Start with a 3-minute animated diagram explanation of each pattern (Singleton, Observer, State Machine) using simple game analogies (e.g., GameManager for Singleton, PlayerHealth/UI for Observer, EnemyAI for State Machine). Follow with 9 minutes of live coding in Unity, demonstrating the implementation of the `GameManager` Singleton with `DontDestroyOnLoad`, the `PlayerHealth` Observer pattern using C# events, and the `EnemyAI` State Machine using an enum and switch statement. Show the effects in the Unity editor (e.g., `GameManager` persisting, debug logs for events, enemy state changes). Include a split-screen view of code and Unity editor. End with an interactive quiz asking learners to identify the best pattern for a given scenario.
